newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia bonds pare fall, rate hopes dashed.
newsitem.headline: Australia bonds pare fall, rate hopes dashed.

text.p: *Australian debt pared some of the sharp price falls that followed today's strong employment data, but any glimmer of hope that an easing was still on the cards has now virtually ended.

Australian debt futures pared some of the sharp falls that followed today's strong employment data, although any glimmer of hope that a monetary policy easing was still on the cards was virtually put to rest.

Bills and short-end bonds sold off rapidly on the news that employment had jumped 38,400 in January, well above market expectations, extending their recent slide on other healthy data and cautious comments by Reserve Bank governor Ian Macfarlane.
March bills fell to 94.05, much in line with 6.0 percent cash rates, but unlike other contracts, it never recovered.
Axiom Funds Management's senior economist, Matthew Drennan, said today's data along with an improving outlook for housing justify the RBA's adoption of a more neutral policy stance.
"The money market has quickly picked up on this change in view, aggressively reducing its bet on another rate cut in March or April," Drennan said.

The case for official rates to stay on hold has been building, particularly over the past week, as November quarter wages growth proved strong and the RBA indicated that it wanted to see the outcome from the trade unions "living wage" claim, all of which has continually put the short-end on the defensive.

"The three official rate cuts have been supplemented by sharper falls in mortgage rates, and the RBA will allow time for these lower rates to work their way through the economy," added John Peters, senior economist at Westpac.

While the March bills wiped out rate cut hopes, the further forward December 1997 bill contract notably dropped to 94.55 on the jobs data, which practically priced in a 50 basis point tightening by year-end.
The sharp rise in employment was not picked up in the unemployment rate, however, which remained at 8.6 percent.

Economists at ANZ Securities agreed that events in the past week makes a rate cut less likely, but "the stubbornly high employment rate means that another cut cannot be totally ruled out," they said in a report.
However, this was provided that the "living wage" claim and enterprise bargaining agreements suggest a subdued outlook for wages and GDP data suggests continued weak activity, they added.
Meanwhile, the long end also weakened on the data, but found support once the 10-year yield spread to the U.S. blew out 100 basis points.

The U.S. faces the last leg of the refunding auctions later today with the sale of US$10.0 billion of 30-year bonds. U.S. Treasuries ended flat on Wednesday amid disappointment of a weak response to the 10-year note sale.
